description: Dev set B: 12 casual, multi-concept questions written from the PDFs (not from Questions.csv). Each item has one casual question, 3 to 5 required terms that a good answer must contain, the source pages and the exact source sentences. Every term and sentence was checked with pdfplumber on the PDFs. Used to measure the text route; no golden item.
page_numbering: pdf_page is the 1-based page of the PDF file, the same numbering as DOCn:pN citations

items.topic: did the crisis hit emerging countries as hard as rich ones
items.question: Did the crisis hit the emerging countries as hard as the rich ones, or did they get off easier?
sentences: Note also that, despite the fact that the crisis originated in the United States, European and emerging market stock prices decreased by as much as their U.S. counterparts; we shall return to this later.
Growth in emerging and developing economies remained positive but was nearly 4 percentage points lower than the 2000–2007 average.
Emerging and developing economies have largely recovered.

items.topic: does the euro suit every member
items.question: Does the euro work just as well for every country that uses it?
sentences: They point out that a common currency means a common monetary policy, which means the same interest rate across the euro countries.
The first country needs lower interest rates to increase spending and output; the second country needs higher interest rates to slow down its economy.
A number of euro members, from Ireland, to Portugal, to Greece, are going through deep recessions.

items.topic: why a euro member cannot lower its own interest rate
items.question: Why can't a country in the euro area just cut its own interest rate when it's in a slump?
sentences: They point out that a common currency means a common monetary policy, which means the same interest rate across the euro countries.
If they had their own currency, they likely would have decreased their interest rate or depreciated their currency vis à vis other euro members to increase the demand for their exports.
Thus, some economists argue that they should drop out of the euro.

items.topic: is very low unemployment always good
items.question: Is really low unemployment always a good thing?
sentences: Like an engine running at too high a speed, an economy in which unemployment is very low may be overutilizing its resources and run into labor shortages.
At the end of 2000, some economists worried that the unemployment rate, 4% at the time, was indeed too low.
But intuition suggests that, when unemployment becomes very low, the economy is likely to overheat, and that this will lead to upward pressure on inflation.

items.topic: is inflation always bad and deflation good
items.question: If inflation is so bad, does that mean falling prices are a good thing?
sentences: If inflation is so bad, does this imply that deflation (negative inflation) is good?
First, high deflation (a large negative rate of inflation) would create many of the same problems as high inflation, from distortions to increased uncertainty.
Second, as we shall see later in the book, even a low rate of deflation limits the ability of monetary policy to affect output.

items.topic: why output per person needs a price adjustment across countries
items.question: Why can't you just compare income per person in dollars between a poor country and a rich one?
sentences: For example, the price of an average restaurant meal in New York City is about 20 dollars; the price of an average restaurant meal in Beijing is about 25 yuans, or, at the current exchange rate, about 4 dollars.
Put another way, the same income (expressed in dollars) buys you much more in Beijing than in New York City.
If we want to compare standards of living, we have to correct for these differences; measures which do so are called PPP (for purchasing power parity) measures.

items.topic: why GDP is not the sum of all sales
items.question: Why isn't GDP just all the sales in the economy added up?
sentences: As the sum of the values of all goods produced in the economy—the sum of $100 from the production of steel and $200 from the production of cars, so $300?
Because steel is an intermediate good: It is used in the production of cars.
We want to count only the production of final goods, not intermediate goods.

items.topic: why the unemployment rate can mislead when jobs are scarce
items.question: Can the unemployment rate make things look better than they really are when jobs are hard to find?
sentences: When unemployment is high, some of the unemployed give up looking for a job and therefore are no longer counted as unemployed.
Equivalently, a higher unemployment rate is typically associated with a lower participation rate, defined as the ratio of the labor force to the total population of working age.

items.topic: do politicians agree on how to cut the U.S. deficit
items.question: Do politicians at least agree on how to fix the U.S. deficit?
sentences: Even if there is agreement on the need for deficit reduction, there is much less agreement on how it should be achieved.
The disagreement is along political lines.
Republicans believe that it should be done primarily through decreases in spending.
Democrats believe that most existing programs are justified, and they are more inclined to want to do the adjustment through an increase in taxes.

items.topic: why 2001 counts as a recession despite positive growth
items.question: How can people call 2001 a recession if the economy still grew that year?
sentences: According to the graph, growth was positive in 2001.
Although GDP growth was positive for 2001 as a whole, it was negative during each of the first three quarters of 2001; thus 2001 qualifies as a (mild) recession.

items.topic: what drives output in the short run versus the long run
items.question: What actually moves output: is it people's demand or stuff like schools and saving?
sentences: Reading newspapers suggests a first answer: Movements in output come from movements in the demand for goods.
This suggests a third answer: The true determinants of output are factors like a country’s education system, its saving rate, and the quality of its government.
In the short run, say, a few years, the first answer is the right one.
In the long run, say, a few decades or more, the third answer is the right one.

items.topic: why China's growth is not a simple recipe for other poor countries
items.question: Can other poor countries just copy what China did to grow so fast?
sentences: China is one of a number of countries that made the transition from central planning to a market economy.
Most of the other countries, from Central Europe to Russia and the other former Soviet republics, experienced a large decrease in output at the time of transition.

Others argue that the fact that the communist party has remained in control has actually helped the economic transition; tight political control has allowed for a better protection of property rights, at least for new firms, giving them incentives to invest.
